title: Paul in Jerusalem: Humility, Hostility, and Defense
content:
Paul in Jerusalem: Humility, Hostility, and Defense

Main Idea: Paul gets attacked by a Jewish mob while participating in a vow, and then he gives a defense speech before the crowd.

Outline

  1. Humility and Love Displayed in James and Paul (21:17-26)
  2. Hostility and Lies Displayed in the Jewish Mob (21:27-36)
  3. Honesty and Loyalty Displayed in Paul's Defense (21:37-22:21)

Humility and Love Displayed in James and Paul (21:17-26)

When Paul arrives in Jerusalem, things get interesting on day two. A formal meeting takes place between Paul, James (Jesus's half brother and primary spokesman of the Jerusalem church), and the Jerusalem elders. In this meeting we find a few wonderful expressions of humility and love.

A God-Centered Celebration (21:18-20a)

James and Paul together praise God for the victories achieved among the Gentiles. "God had done" the work among them (v. 19). Paul didn't brag; he gave glory to God. He also related "in detail" what God did on his journeys, not to receive praise but to celebrate the evidences of God's grace and to share them with others.

When the Jewish Christians heard these things, they too "glorified God" (v. 20). Their joyful reaction is similar to previous reactions when the Jewish Christians received reports of God's grace shown to Cornelius, the Greeks in Antioch, and in the first missionary journey (11:18; 22:29; 14:27; 15:12).

A Grace-Motivated Gift

At some point, in response to the grace of Jesus, certain Christians presented a love offering to the church in Jerusalem. This gift accomplished two purposes: it served as a means of helping the poor (cf. Acts 11:27-30; 2 Corinthians 8-9; Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:16), and it also served as a symbol of unity.

A Gospel-Driven Plan (21:20b-26)

The great news was that thousands of Jews trusted in Christ (v. 20b). But what hurt Paul's reputation was that many of these believers were zealous about continuing to keep Jewish customs while the word on the street was that Paul was urging Jewish Christians who lived in Gentile communities to abandon their heritage.

James's concern wasn't about salvation. He and Paul agreed that salvation was by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. The concern was about what Paul was teaching the Gentile cities. James proposed that Paul demonstrate his respect for traditional Jewish observances by participating in a purification ritual.

Paul's ultimate motivation was the gospel (20:24). He sacrificed his safety and his freedom for its sake. Paul could have said, "Let the haters hate. I'm going to do what I want." But he didn't. He submitted to James's proposal in hopes of unifying the church and advancing the gospel. He lived out his words: "To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win Jews; to those under the law, like one under the law, though I myself am not under the law" (1 Corinthians 9:20).

We too should be flexible when ministering to various cultures. Some cultures are more traditional, while others are more progressive. When outside your immediate sphere, you must find all necessary ways to adapt to the ways of another group for the sake of the gospel's advancement.

Hostility and Lies Displayed in the Jewish Mob (21:27-36)

From its focus on humility and love, Acts 21 turns to hostility and lies. We find a stark contrast between the spirit of Paul and the spirit of the Jewish crowd in verses 27-36. Some Asian Jews (probably from Ephesus) first recognized Paul and responded violently to him (vv. 27-28). Their accusations against him were designed to generate mob violence.

The charges sounded like what Stephen's accusers said: lies about someone going to bring death (6:13-14). All the accusations are even more ironic given that Paul was actually undergoing a purification ritual in order to enter the temple!

The Jews asserted that Paul was defiling the temple by bringing Trophimus the Ephesian (v. 29; cf. 20:4) beyond the wall that separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner sanctuary, which was off limits to Gentiles (Ephesians 2:14). Of course, he had done no such thing. Paul's punishment for this violation was the death penalty.

As a result of these claims, the crowd became hostile and tried to kill Paul. Fortunately, the Roman soldiers (stationed nearby, knowing that the temple area could be a volatile place) heard the wild uproar. Lysias, the commander, had the responsibility of maintaining peace in the area, and he proceeds to arrest Paul and put the apostle in "two chains" (v. 33), perhaps indicating that he bound his hands and feet, as Agabus predicted (v. 11).

Honesty and Loyalty Displayed in Paul's Defense (21:37-22:21)

When the mob reaches the steps of the Antonia fortress, the soldiers had to lift Paul up and carry him in order to protect him from the angry mob (v. 35). The crowd continued to chant, "Get rid of him!" (v. 36), just as an earlier crowd in Jerusalem demanded of Pontius Pilate, "Take this man away!" (Luke 23:18) and "Crucify him!" (Mark 15:13).

Paul informs Lysias that he is neither a terrorist nor an Egyptian, but a Jew and a citizen of the honorable city of Tarsus (v. 39). Lysias grants Paul permission to speak. Paul stands at the top of the steps, and the crowd falls silent as Paul addresses them in their own language ("Hebrew dialect," i.e. Aramaic; 21:40; cf. 22:2; 26:14).

Former Zeal (22:3-5)

Paul begins by identifying with the crowd, reflecting on his former life. He was born a Jew in Tarsus and had been brought up in Jerusalem. He sat at the feet of Gamaliel. He had been a strict Pharisee, indeed the sternest persecutor of Christians (Philippians 3:4-7). His zeal was experienced in the shame and persecution of Christians, both men and women, he who had handled them to death (cf. Acts 8:3; 26:10). Paul wanted to destroy Christianity. The high priest and council of elders could confirm his story (22:5). They knew that at one time Paul had even sought to travel all the way to Damascus to pursue followers of the Way.

Encounter with Jesus (22:6-11)

But then something happened: Paul met the living Christ, and that changed everything. Paul around noon implies it confirms (for the audience) that he was truly seeing a light from heaven. Paul fell to the ground and heard Jesus speaking to him. Paul includes in his defense speech that it was Jesus of Nazareth who confronted him.

Commission (22:12-16)

Paul goes on to describe Ananias's devotion to the law, adding the note that Ananias "had a good reputation with all the Jews" (v. 12). Paul's mention of Ananias is part of God's purpose in this defense speech. Paul wants to emphasize his respect for Israel.

Let's consider four parts to Paul's commission:

  1. "The God of our ancestors called Paul" (22:14). This is the language God used in Moses's burning bush experience (Exodus 3:15-16). The same God who commissioned Moses also commissioned Paul.
  2. God also highlights God's marvelous grace. Did Moses deserve to hear God's voice and be used to bring people into freedom? No. Did Paul deserve such grace? Did he deserve the privilege of proclaiming liberty to the nations? No. Both men were dependent on grace.
  3. God appointed Paul to be "the Righteous One" (22:14). This too is an allusion to the Old Testament, stressing the continuity between the Old Testament and the work of Jesus the Messiah. Isaiah speaks of the Righteous One as the obedient Servant who was wounded for our transgressions.
  4. God called Paul to be his "witness" to "all people" (22:15; cf. v. 21; 26:17; Galatians 1:16). The man would give eyewitness testimony (1 Corinthians 9:1) to people of all ethnicities and social classes.

Vision in the Temple (22:17-21)

In the last part of Paul's defense speech, he tells of the vision he had in the temple. This part of Paul's story doesn't appear in Acts 9 (cf. 9:26-30). He probably included it here in order to answer the mob's charge that he had defiled the temple. He had no interest in defiling the very place he prayed in it!

In some ways Paul's vision sounds similar to Isaiah's vision (Isaiah 6:1-13), once again showing continuity between Judaism and the Christian faith. Both men were called through a vision and were commissioned (22:18-21). Both were told that many people would reject their message.

Paul describes how he protested the vision, which is another element connecting him to narrowing figures in the Old Testament. Paul argued he should stay in Jerusalem because (unlike those he previously persecuted) Christians in Jerusalem would listen to his testimony (v. 19). Despite the argument the Lord persisted and said, "Go, because I will send you far away to the Gentiles" (v. 21). This calling to the Gentiles wasn't merely for the sake of safety but as a matter of purpose. The Lord had raised Paul up specifically so that he would be a witness to the Gentiles.

Key Takeaways from Paul's Defense

  1. Paul responds with gentleness and compassion. He doesn't respond in anger. He doesn't attack. He reasons. When you are in a pressure-filled conversation, ask the Father to calm you and give you grace to speak the message with gentleness and respect (cf. Galatians 5:22-25; 2 Timothy 2:24-26; 1 Peter 3:15).
  2. We can learn from Paul's courage. In the face of opposition, Paul didn't bend. He stood his ground. Such boldness also comes from God (cf. Acts 4:29-31). Many Christians can remain calm, but that's because they cave in and fail to speak truth when pressed. We need both truth and love (cf. Ephesians 4:15). Only churches that love people and stand firm on the gospel against the winds of culture will have anything to offer this broken world.
  3. We can learn from Paul's calling. Paul knew his assignment: to proclaim the good news. That's our job too. On this particular occasion, the crowd is enraged against the apostle. On other occasions in Acts, however, people respond to his words in faith. We aren't responsible for the results of what happens when we lovingly proclaim the good news; we are responsible for sharing it.

While some people plant the seeds of the gospel through proclamation and others water it through active discipleship and deeper teaching that reinforces the message, only God gives growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Sometimes people will be enraged by a presentation of the gospel; sometimes people will hear it and inquire for more information; and sometimes people will surrender to the lordship of Jesus.

Discussion Questions

  1. What does it mean to defend the faith?
  2. When might you need to defend the faith?
  3. How do Paul and James display humility and love?
  4. Compare Acts 21:20b-26 with 1 Corinthians 9:15-23. Are Paul's actions and his missionary policy consistent? Explain your answer.
  5. Why were the Jewish people enraged at Paul?
  6. In what situations might Christians face hostility and false accusations? How should we respond to them?
  7. Generally speaking, what does Paul try to accomplish in his defense speech in Acts 22?
  8. How is Paul's calling similar to the callings of Moses and Isaiah? How is it different?
  9. Do you think Paul's speech was effective? Explain.
  10. Take a few moments to pray for God to help you present the gospel this week. Ask God to bring your hearers to faith in Christ.
